hops.afterHeading: What transduces force in the lung and the artery
hops.title: Count your pulse sitting, then standing
hops.text: Sit for a minute, rest two fingertips on the inside of your wrist, and count your pulse for fifteen seconds. Then stand up and count again. Heart rate typically rises by about 10 to 15 beats per minute on standing, so you may count a few extra beats. Standing lets gravity shift 500 to 800 millilitres of blood into your legs and abdomen. Wall stretch at the carotid sinus and aortic arch drops, the baroreceptors fire less, and the brainstem eases the vagal brake while turning up sympathetic drive. If standing up ever makes you feel faint, skip this one.

sources.citation: Campos Munoz A, Vohra S, Gupta M. Orthostasis. StatPearls, 2023 (PMID 30422533)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A college student standing by a sunlit desk, checking their wrist pulse with two fingertips.
image.caption: Standing shifts blood to the legs, arterial stretch falls, baroreceptors fire less, and the heart speeds up.

hops.title: Oto-tricho-tussia: when a stray hair in the ear canal sets off a cough
hops.text: A 51-year-old man had over six weeks of coughing spasms that resisted antibiotics, a steroid inhaler and reflux pills. Ear specialists found a single hair on his eardrum. Removing it stopped his throat tickle at once, he reported. A small branch of the vagus, Arnold's nerve, carries touch from the ear canal to the brainstem, where it can set off the cough reflex. In one study, swabbing the ear canal made 2 percent of healthy volunteers cough, against 25.5 percent of adults with chronic cough. The case authors proposed the name oto-tricho-tussia (ear, hair, cough).

sources.citation: Castro RA, Zalvan CH, Berzofsky C. Oto-tricho-tussia: hair in the ear canal as a cause of chronic cough. Case Reports in Otolaryngology, 2020 (PMC7150714)
Dicpinigaitis PV, Kantar A, Enilari O, Paravati F. Prevalence of Arnold nerve reflex in adults and children with chronic cough. Chest, 2018 (PMID 29197546)

image.caption: A stray hair on the eardrum can stimulate the vagus nerve's ear branch and, in some people, set off coughing.

hops.afterHeading: From afferent to behaviour: stretch, satiety and what the trial evidence covers
hops.title: Why chicken soup fills you more than chicken with a glass of water
hops.text: In a 1999 study, 24 women ate a 1,128-kilojoule chicken-and-rice starter 17 minutes before lunch. A casserole with a 356-gram glass of water on the side did no better than the casserole alone. After a soup made from the same ingredients and water, the women ate 27 percent fewer calories at lunch than after casserole and water, with no catch-up eating at dinner. A 2012 Nottingham study used roast chicken and vegetables. On MRI, water drunk with the solid meal left the stomach quickly, while the blended soup kept stomach volume up longer; in a separate group, the soup lowered hunger.

sources.citation: Rolls BJ, Bell EA, Thorwart ML. Water incorporated into a food but not served with a food decreases energy intake in lean women. Am J Clin Nutr, 1999 (PMID 10500012)
Marciani L et al. Preventing gastric sieving by blending a solid/water meal enhances satiation in healthy humans. J Nutr, 2012 (PMID 22649258)

image.caption: Blended into soup, the water stays with the food, so the stomach stays fuller for longer.

audio.title: A hair, a collar and a bowl of soup
audio.transcript:
About eighty percent of the vagus nerve's fibres carry sensory signals toward the brain, by one standard estimate. Here are three real cases where touch and stretch sensors give themselves away, moving down the body from the ear, to the neck, to the stomach.

First, the ear. In a twenty twenty case report, a fifty-one-year-old man had coughing spasms for more than six weeks. Antibiotics, an inhaled steroid and reflux medication changed nothing. Then ear specialists looked into his left ear canal and found a single strand of hair lying on his eardrum. When it was removed, the tickle in his throat stopped immediately, he reported. How can a hair in the ear cause a cough? A small branch of the vagus, called Arnold's nerve, carries touch from the ear canal to the brainstem, where it can trigger the cough reflex. In a twenty eighteen study, touching the ear canal with a cotton-tipped applicator made two percent of healthy volunteers cough, compared with twenty-five point five percent of adults with chronic cough. The authors suggest this reflects vagal hypersensitivity in chronic cough. The case authors proposed a name for the condition, oto-tricho-tussia, which means ear, hair, cough.

Second, move down to the carotid artery in the neck. Arterial baroreceptors do not read a pressure gauge. They detect stretch in the vessel wall and report it to the brainstem, here through a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve. In carotid sinus syndrome, seen mostly in older adults, the reflex responds too strongly to pressure on the neck, and why is not well understood. Pressure from a tight shirt collar, or from shaving, can be enough to trigger it, and the person may feel dizzy or faint. Doctors test for it by massaging the carotid sinus for about ten seconds while monitoring heart rhythm and blood pressure. A marked pause in the heartbeat or drop in blood pressure on its own only shows hypersensitivity, not the syndrome. Diagnosing the syndrome requires a history of otherwise unexplained fainting compatible with a reflex mechanism, and an abnormal pause or drop in blood pressure during the test that reproduces the person's usual symptoms. The pause is the vagal part: the brainstem applies the vagal brake to the heart. A collar setting off a blood-pressure reflex fits with a sensor that responds to mechanical deformation.

Third, the stomach, which tracks stretch alongside nutrients. In a nineteen ninety-nine study, twenty-four women ate the same starter seventeen minutes before lunch: one thousand one hundred twenty-eight kilojoules of chicken and rice, about two hundred seventy calories. On one day it came as a casserole, on another as a casserole with three hundred fifty-six grams of water on the side, and on another as a soup with the same ingredients and the same amount of water. The glass of water on the side made no difference to lunch. After the soup, the women ate twenty-seven percent fewer calories at lunch than after the casserole with water, with no catch-up eating at dinner. In twenty twelve, researchers in Nottingham used M R I to watch the stomachs of eighteen volunteers who ate roast chicken and vegetables with a glass of water. The stomach sieved the water out past the solids, so stomach volume fell fast. Blending the same meal into soup kept the water with the food and slowed that fall. In a separate group of twenty-two volunteers, the soup lowered hunger. Stomach stretch and gut hormones may both contribute.

A stray hair, a tight collar and a bowl of soup: three reminders that sensory nerves report touch and stretch to your brainstem all day.
